'''''Oxybasis chenopodioides''''' (syn. ''Chenopodium chenopodioides'') is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Amaranthaceae]] known by the common name '''saltmarsh goosefoot''' (or '''low goosefoot''' in America). It is native to Europe, Asia and parts of Africa, where it grows on bare mud in brackish hollows in coastal grassland, inland salt steppes and salty deserts. It has spread to similar habitats in both North and South America. Its habitat is an uncommon one and is threatened by agricultural improvement in many areas, but overall its populations are stable. This species often grows with, and is easily confused with the closely related [[Oxybasis rubra|red goosefoot]].

==Description==
Saltmarsh Goosefoot is an annual [[herbaceous plant|herb]], up about 30 cm (sometimes as much as 50 cm) tall, but often growing prostrate along the ground. Its roots are short and fibrous, and the whole plant is easily lifted out of the soil. The stem is angular and often branched towards the base, with the branches generally occurring in (subopposite) pairs. The whole plant is glabrous (hairless), albeit sometimes with mealy vesicular hairs on the leaves, and it can be either green or crimson in colour (often both).<ref name=Sell1>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 1 |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>

The leaves are alternate, with a short (ca. 0.8 cm) petiole and no stipules. The leaf blades can be up to 8 cm long by 6 cm wide, but are usually much smaller than this, typically 2–3 cm long. The lamina is quite thick and fleshy, triangular to ovate in outline, and will be either entire (untoothed) or just with a few obscure teeth on the margin.<ref name="Sell1" /><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>
[[File:Oxybasis chenopodioides Seasalter.jpg|thumb|A small plant exhibiting typical colouration]]

Flowering occurs from July to September in northern Europe. The inflorescences are technically [[panicle]]s, with a branched structure and clusters of glomerules (bunches of flowers on very short stalks) but they often look like spikes (sessile flowers on a single stem). The glomerules consist of 10-20 small, red flowers of two types: the terminal ones are bisexual, with 5 [[tepal]]s, 5 [[stamen]]s and 2 [[Stigma (botany)|stigmas]]; the lateral ones can be bisexual or female with 3-5 tepals and 0-3 stamens. The fruit is an [[achene]] which falls while still contained within the [[perianth]].<ref name="Sell1" /><ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref>
[[File:Chenopodium chenopodioides sl28.jpg|thumb|The flowers have 3-5 purplish tepals forming an almost closed ball]]

==Taxonomy==
The original name (basionym) of this species was ''Blitum chenopodioides'', as coined by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in his work [http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/spa/Libro.php?Libro=947 Mantissa plantarum] in 1771. Under the Linnaean system, the genus ''Blitum'' was differentiated from ''Chenopodium'' by having just one (rather than five) [[stamen]]s. This strict reliance on flower structure declined with time, however, and it has until recently been known as ''Chenopodium chenopodioides'', the name assigned to it by Paul Aellen in 1933. However, in 2012, an analysis of the relationships of the many species in the [[Chenopodioideae]] by Susy Fuentes-Bazan and colleagues resulted in its reassignment to the new genus ''Oxybasis'', along with [[Oxybasis rubra|red goosefoot]] and some related plants.<ref name=GBIF>{{Cite web |title=''Oxybasis chenopodioides'' (L.) S.Fuentes, Uotila & Borsch |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/8117283 |access-date=25 November 2023 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref><ref name=Fuentes>{{Cite journal |last1=Fuentes-Bazan |first1=S. |last2=Uotila |first2=P. |last3=Borsch |first3=T. |date=2012 |title=A novel phylogeny-based generic classification for Chenopodium sensu lato, and a tribal rearrangement of Chenopodioideae (Chenopodiaceae) |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.3372/wi42.42101 |journal=Willdenowia |volume=42 |pages=5–24|doi=10.3372/wi42.42101 }}</ref>

A large number of other synonyms have been coined over the years, most notably ''Blitum botryoides'' (by Solomon Drejer in 1877) and ''B. crassifolium'' (by Heinrich Reichenbach in 1832). A full list is given in [https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77121017-1 Plants of the World Online].<ref name="GBIF" />

Several subspecies and varieties have been named over the years but none is currently accepted, although Sell & Murrell recently described var. ''lengyleianum'' <small>Aellen</small> as an erect and richly branched plant, while var. ''degenianum'' <small>Aellen</small> is a prostrate form. They may be kept separate by self-pollination.<ref name="Sell1" />

Its chromosome number is 2''n'' = 18,<ref name="Stace"/> but it often exhibits endopolyploidy, where certain somatic cells have more than one set of chromosomes, often as an adaptation to stress.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Skaptsov |first1=M.V. |last2=Lomonosova |first2=M.N. |last3=Kutseva |first3=M.G. |date=2017 |title=The phenomenon of endopolyploidy in some species of the Chenopodioideae (Amaranthaceae) |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/23818107.2016.1276475 |journal=Botany Letters |volume=164 |issue=1 |pages=47–53|doi=10.1080/23818107.2016.1276475 |bibcode=2017BotL..164...47S |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The generic name ''Oxybasis'' was coined by Grigorij Karelin and Ivan Kirilov in 1841,<ref name="Fuentes" /> while ''chenopodioides'' means "like a [[Chenopodium|goosefoot]]." In England it is known as saltmarsh goosefoot, while Americans call it low goosefoot or buttered goosefoot.<ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?3084,3147,3155 Jepson Manual Treatment]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Low Goosefoot |url=https://wildflowersearch.org/search?&PlantName=Chenopodium+chenopodioides |access-date=25 November 2023 |website=Wildflower Search}}</ref>

==Identification==
Saltmarsh goosefoot can be very difficult to separate from [[Oxybasis rubra|red goosefoot]]. Under normal circumstances, saltmarsh goosefoot is a low-growing plant with almost entire leaves, whereas red goosefoot is a much larger, erect plant with very definite leaf lobes and teeth. However, both plants are variable in these regards and sometimes they are almost indistinguishable. Either species can be predominantly red or green in colour. The key difference is that the tepals of the lateral fruits are fused to nearly the tip in saltmarsh goosefoot (i.e. forming an almost complete ball), while those of red goosefoot are only fused half way, allowing more of the seed to be seen. This character should be used when the fruit are mature.<ref name="Stace" /><ref name="Sell1" />

{{Image frame|width=424|content=[[File:Chenopodium chenopodioides sl27.jpg|200px]] [[File:Chenopodium rubrum (s. str.) sl27.jpg|200px]]|caption=Flowers of saltmarsh goosefoot (left), with fused tepals, and red goosefoot (right), with separate tepals|align=center}}

==Distribution and status==
Saltmarsh goosefoot is native to southern Europe, Asia and parts of North Africa, and widely established throughout the Americas.<ref name="POWO" /> In central to southern Africa it is known from Kenya, Burundi, Namibia and South Africa<ref name="GBIF" /> and it has recently been added to the flora of the [[Congo Basin|Congo]] from a specimen collected in 1914. It is thought to have been carried to this region by migrating birds, which would make it a [[native species]] there, albeit on the edge of its range.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sukhorukov |first1=Alexander |last2=Kushunina |first2=Maria |last3=Verloove |first3=Filip |date=2016 |title=Notes on Atriplex, Oxybasis and Dysphania (Chenopodiaceae) in West-Central Tropical Africa |journal=Plant Ecology and Evolution |volume=149 |issue=2 |pages=249–256|doi=10.5091/plecevo.2016.1181 |bibcode=2016PlEcE.149..249S |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In the United States, by contrast, it is usually considered to be a casual, presumably introduced by humans. It has occurred in New York since at least 1894, but it dies out quite quickly.<ref>{{Cite web |date=3 December 2023 |title=Oxybasis chenopodioides |url=https://newyork.plantatlas.usf.edu/plant.aspx?id=6312 |website=New York Flora Atlas}}</ref> In western North America it is well established in the Rocky Mountains, from British Columbia to California, where it grows in [[sagebrush]] desert vegetation, usually on roadsides.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oxybasis chenopodioides, low goosefoot, red goosefoot |url=https://burkeherbarium.org/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Oxybasis%20chenopodioides |access-date=3 December 2023 |website=Burke Herbarium Image Collection}}</ref>

Some American publications state that "low goosefoot" is a native of South America,<ref name="Jepson">{{cite web |last1=Clemants |first1=Steven E. |last2=Benet-Pierce |first2=Nuri |title=''Chenopodium chenopodioides'' |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=19152 |website=Jepson Flora Project (eds.) Jepson eFlora |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |access-date=30 November 2023 |date=2012}}</ref> where it has been known since at least 1891, when it was collected at [[Soriano Department|Soriano]] in Uruguay.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Flora Fanerogamica Argentina |url=http://www.floraargentina.edu.ar/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/40-CHENOPODIACEAE.pdf |access-date=4 December 2023 |website=Flora Argentina y del Cono Sur}}</ref> It is sometimes considered to be a plant of the coast of Argentina, but there are few records of it there.<ref name="GBIF" />
[[File:lowgoosefootplant.jpg|thumb]]

In France, ''Oxybaside faux chénopode'' occurs mainly around the coast and has a [[IUCN Red List|status]] of LC (Least Concern) in Corsica and the southern départements, but it is considered VU (Vulnerable) in the [[Pas-de-Calais|Nord-Pas-de-Calais]] and CR (critically rare) in [[Picardy|Picardie]]. It is also vulnerable inland, in  [[Lorraine]].<ref name="INPN">{{Cite web |title=Oxybaside faux chénopode, Oxybasis faux chénopode, Chénopode à feuilles grasses, Épinard-fraise faux chénopode, Chénopode faux chénopode (Français) |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/717358 |access-date=4 December 2023 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref>

It is considered to be rare in Italy, where it is distributed around the coast of the mainland, Sicily and Sardinia, but is restricted by the lack of suitable habitat.<ref name=Iamonico>{{Cite journal |last=Iamonico |first=D. |date=2014 |title=Taxonomical, morphological, ecological and chorological notes on ''Oxybasis chenopodioides'' and ''O. rubra'' (Chenopodiaceae) in Italy. |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272558071 |journal=Hacquetia |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=285–296 |doi=10.2478/hacq-2014-0004|bibcode=2014Hacq...13..285I |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The first British record (as ''Chenopodium botryodes'' <small>Sm.</small>) was published by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|J.E. Smith]] in ''[[English Botany]]'' in 1811.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Clarke |first1=W.A. |title=First Records of British Flowering Plants |date=1900 |publisher=West, Newman & Co. |location=London}}</ref> In 1962 it was shown to be largely confined to coastal grasslands in the south east of England ([[Kent]] and [[Essex]]),<ref name=Perring>{{cite book |last1=Perring |first1=F.H. | last2=Walters |first2=S.M. |title=Atlas of the British Flora |date=1962 |publisher=Thomas Nelson and Sons Ltd. |location=Edinburgh}}</ref> and that has not changed since then. It is currently considered to be nationally scarce, but not threatened, with an IUCN status of LC (Least Concern).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Saltmarsh Goosefoot Oxybasis chenopodioides |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vewmh1 |access-date=6 December 2023 |website=Plant Atlas 2020}}</ref> It is regarded as an [[axiophyte]] of conservation habitats.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kent Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2023/11/Kent-Axiophytes-v2-20231.pdf |access-date=6 December 2023 |website=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland}}</ref>

The [https://www.gbif.org/species/8117283 Global Biodiversity Information Forum] map shows saltmarsh goosefoot extending across the central [[steppe]] of Asia as far as eastern [[Siberia]]. It just extends into China in parts of the [[Gobi Desert]], where it is found in salt flats.<ref name="efloras">{{cite web |title=''Chenopodium chenopodioides'' |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200006814 |website=Flora of China @ efloras.org |access-date=30 November 2023}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
The usual habitat for saltmarsh goosefoot is not in salt marsh at all, but in grasslands with some brackish influence, often close to coasts. It is typically found in shallow depressions, where winter flooding lasts into the spring, creating patches of bare ground. It is late to germinate and only flowers in the autumn, so a lack of competition is important. Inland, it is usually associated with natural salt deposits or possibly with salt-treated roadside verges.

Under the [[European Environment Agency|EUNIS]] habitat classification system, saltmarsh goosefoot is a characteristic plant of the [[Pannonian Basin|Pannonic]] salt steppes of south-east Europe, and specifically of the salty E6.2131 ''[[Puccinellia distans]]'' hollows that are found in this type of grassland. In this inland vegetation, it is evaporation of surface water in dry summers that creates the brackish conditions, rather than the influence of the sea, and the salts are mainly carbonates and sulphates rather than chlorides.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Polunin |first1=Oleg |title=A Guide to the Vegetation of Britain and Europe |last2=Walters |first2=Martin |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1985 |isbn=0-19-217713-3 |location=Oxford}}</ref> This is a priority habitat, and many [[Natura 2000]] sites are designated for its protection.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pannonic salt steppes and salt marshes |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/habitats/10029 |access-date=9 December 2023 |website=European Nature Information System}}</ref>

The equivalent habitats in southern France are the halo-nitrophile lawns of the Mediterranean coasts of the mainland and [[Corsica]] ([[Coordination of Information on the Environment|Corine]] code 22.343), which are also a priority habitat for conservation. This vegetation is found in grazed pastures, and contains such species as [[Atriplex prostrata|spear-leaved orache]], [[Polypogon monspeliensis|annual beard-grass]] and [[Corrigiola litoralis|strapwort]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 December 2023 |title=Gazons méditerranéens amphibies halonitrophiles (Heleochloion) |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/docs/cahab/habitats-declines/3170_3.pdf |website=Inventaire National do Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref> Its [[Phytosociology|vegetation communities]] include [[Juncus bufonius|toad rush]]-saltmarsh goosefoot community (mainly on the Atlantic coast),<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=de Foucault |first1=B. |last2=Bioret |first2=F. |date=2010 |title=Contribution au prodrome des végétations de France: les ''Saginetea maritimae'' Westhoff et al. 1962 |url=https://habref-web.mnhn.fr/uploads/sources/TYPO_PVF2_PDF_60_SAGINETEA_JB50_2010.pdf |journal=J. Bot. Soc. Bot. France |volume=50 |pages=59–83}}</ref> and ''[[Echinochloa crus-galli]]''-''[[Sporobolus schoenoides]]'' and ''[[Gnaphalium uliginosum]]''-''Sporobolus schoenoides'' vegetation on the Mediterranean.<ref name="INPN" />

In Italy the typical habitat appears slightly different. It is found on sandy, almost bare soils which are inundated in the winter and dry out in summer, allowing for a 4-month growing season from August to November. It usually occurs on the coast, in association with plants such as ''Salicornia perennans'' and ''[[Suaeda maritima]]'', but is sometimes found inland at heights up to 180 m.<ref name="Iamonico" />

Britain is at the northern edge of its natural range, and saltmarsh goosefoot is largely restricted to the grazing marshes of the [[Thames Estuary]], where it grows on the banks of brackish ditches that are poached by cattle, or in shallow rills in the fields, which dry out in the summer.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Williams |first=P. |title=A survey of ditch flora in the North Kent Marshes SSSIs - 1995. English Nature Research Report No. 167 |publisher=English Nature |year=1996 |location=Peterborough |url=https://archive.org/details/north-kent-ditches-survey-1995}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Jermyn |first=S.T. |title=Flora of Essex |publisher=Essex Naturalists' Trust Limited |year=1974 |isbn=0-904768-01-5 |location=Colchester}}</ref> Populations fluctuate dramatically with the weather, flourishing only after a hot summer.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kitchener |first=G.D. |date=2021 |title=Kent Rare Plant Register: Oxybasis chenopodioides (L.) S. Fuentes, Uotila & Borsch (Chenopodium chenopodioides (L.) Aellen) (Saltmarsh Goosefoot) |url=https://bsbi.org/kent |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121210000000/https://bsbi.org/kent |archive-date=10 December 2012 |website=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland}} [https://archive.org/details/oxybasis-chenopodioides-kent-rpr Alt URL]</ref> It is sufficiently rare that it is not described in any vegetation community;<ref name=Rodwell>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vols. 1-5 |date=1991–2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref> nor does it have any known insect associations.<ref name=PIDB>{{cite web |last1=Biological Records Centre |title=Insects and their food plants |url=http://dbif.brc.ac.uk/ |access-date=10 December 2023}}</ref><ref name=redfern>{{cite journal |last1=Redfern |first1=Margaret |last2=Shirley |first2=Peter |title=British Plant Galls |journal=Field Studies |date=2002 |volume=10 |pages=207–531 |isbn=1-85153-214-5}}</ref>
